igcse-0580-graphs-functions-straight-lin.description: Substitute signed inputs, plot their ordered pairs to scale and read coordinates back from a line.

sections.title: How do I make a table of values?
sections.label: Substitute the signed input
sections.intro: Each column pairs one x-value with its output. Substitute that number into the rule everywhere x occurs.

blocks.html: For a rule of the form \(y=ax+b\), first multiply by \(a\) and then add \(b\). A negative input belongs inside brackets when you substitute.

blocks.title: Complete a table for an increasing straight line
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=3x+2\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(-4\)?\(2\)?\(8\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the x-value by the coefficient of x, then add the constant.

For \(x=-1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-1\).

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=5\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(-4\)\(-1\)\(2\)\(5\)\(8\)

blocks.html: The first value in the pair is x even when it is negative. Do not reorder the pair to put the positive number first.

blocks.title: Use negative inputs for a falling line
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=-3x+3\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)?\(6\)\(3\)\(0\)?
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Bracket a negative input. The product of two negative numbers is positive.

For \(x=-2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=9\).

For \(x=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-3\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(9\)\(6\)\(3\)\(0\)\(-3\)

blocks.html: Check an easy input such as \(x=0\) before plotting the whole table.

sections.title: How do I place each point on the grid?
sections.label: Read both scales
sections.intro: Find the distance between two numbered grid lines. Count the smaller divisions on each axis separately.

blocks.html: Start at the x-coordinate, then move to the y-height. Use crosses for the table points. When the rule is linear, join the points with one straight line.

figure.alt: A scaled straight-line graph passes through the table points at x negative one, zero, one, and two.
figure.caption: Each cross matches one table column. From x equal to 2, the plotted height is 1.

blocks.title: Read the vertical value on a straight line
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=2x-3\). Read the value of \(y\) at \(x=2\).
blocks.hint: Start at the given input on the horizontal axis. Read the other coordinate at the graph.
blocks.solution:
Find \(x=2\) on the horizontal scale.

Move vertically to the graph and then horizontally to the vertical scale. The point is \(\left(2,1\right)\).

blocks.html: An equal distance on the paper need not represent an equal number of x-units and y-units.

blocks.title: Read the input at a stated level
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=-3x+3\). Use the graph to find \(x\) when \(y=0\).
blocks.hint: Start from the given height on the vertical axis.
blocks.solution:
Read the vertical axis at \(y=0\).

Move horizontally to the graph, then down or up to the x-axis. The reading is \(x=1\).

blocks.html: If one point does not lie on the line through the others, recalculate that table entry.

sections.title: How do I read an input, output or intersection?
sections.label: Follow the correct axis first
sections.intro: When x is given, start on the horizontal axis. When y is given, start on the vertical axis.

blocks.html: Follow a grid line to reach the graph, then read the missing coordinate on the other axis. A line intersection is the ordered pair shared by both lines.

blocks.title: Read both coordinates at a line intersection
blocks.prompt: Read the coordinates where the graphs of \(y=2x-1\) and \(y=-3x+9\) meet.
blocks.hint: At the intersection the same ordered pair lies on both lines.
blocks.solution:
Find the point common to both lines. It has the same x- and y-coordinates on both graphs.

Read the horizontal value first and the vertical value second. The point is \(\left(2,3\right)\).

blocks.html: A horizontal line holds y constant. Its different points still have different x-values.

blocks.title: Recognise the constant value shown on a grid
blocks.prompt: Choose the equation of the plotted line.
blocks.hint: Read which coordinate stays constant as you move along the line.
blocks.solution:
Every plotted input shares the height \(3\).

The equation is \(y=3\). This is a horizontal line.

blocks.html: State both coordinates in the order \((x,y)\) for an intersection point.

revision.body:
Substitute the signed input

Substitute each input, keeping any negative sign inside brackets.

Read both scales

Plot the table pairs using both scales. A linear rule gives a straight line.

Follow the correct axis first

For a known input, move vertically to the line. For a known output, move horizontally.

Example

For \(y=2x-3\), the points \(\left(-1,-5\right)\) and \(\left(2,1\right)\) lie on the same straight line.

Check yourself

  • Find y when \(x=-2\) in the example rule.
  • What coordinate stays constant on the horizontal line \(y=4\)?

Answers \(y=-7\), and the y-coordinate.
revision.checks:
• The first value in the pair is x even when it is negative. Do not reorder the pair to put the positive number first.
  • An equal distance on the paper need not represent an equal number of x-units and y-units.
  • A horizontal line holds y constant. Its different points still have different x-values.

igcse-0580-graphs-functions-quadratic-pl.description: Make tables for positive and negative quadratic rules, plot a smooth curve and read heights or intercepts.

sections.title: How do I handle a negative value in a squared term?
sections.label: Square before applying the sign
sections.intro: A negative input gives a positive square. A separate minus sign in front of that square still makes its term negative.

blocks.html: At \(x=-2\), the term \(-x^2\) is \(-(-2)^2=-4\). The term \(3x\) is \(3(-2)=-6\). Add the terms only after giving each its sign.

blocks.title: Substitute negative inputs in an upward quadratic
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=x^{2}+4x-1\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-3\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)
\(y\)?\(-4\)\(-5\)?\(-1\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Put each negative input in brackets before squaring. Evaluate the squared and linear terms separately.

For \(x=-4\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-1\).

For \(x=-1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-4\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-3\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)
\(y\)\(-1\)\(-4\)\(-5\)\(-4\)\(-1\)

blocks.html: For a rule such as \(y=3-x^2\), a negative input does not make the squared term positive after the outer subtraction.

blocks.title: Evaluate a quadratic with a negative squared term
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=-x^{2}+4x+3\).

\(x\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)\(4\)
\(y\)\(3\)?\(7\)\(6\)?
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Square the bracketed input first. Then apply the minus sign in front of the square.

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=6\).

For \(x=4\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=3\).

\(x\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)\(4\)
\(y\)\(3\)\(6\)\(7\)\(6\)\(3\)

blocks.html: Calculate a middle input and a negative input in full before completing the others.

sections.title: How do I join the plotted points?
sections.label: Plot crosses and draw one smooth curve
sections.intro: Each pair in a quadratic table locates a cross. A smooth quadratic may curve between the printed x-values.

blocks.html: Join the plotted crosses with a single smooth curve. If values at opposite distances from the middle line are equal, use that as a check on the table and the drawing.

figure.alt: A downward quadratic is plotted with crosses from negative three to positive three.
figure.caption: The points at x equal to −2 and 2 have the same height. The curve is continuous between the table values.

blocks.title: Read a quadratic height from the two scales
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=x^{2}-4x+7\). Read the value of \(y\) at \(x=3\).
blocks.hint: Start at the given input on the horizontal axis. Read the other coordinate at the graph.
blocks.solution:
Find \(x=3\) on the horizontal scale.

Move vertically to the graph and then horizontally to the vertical scale. The point is \(\left(3,4\right)\).

blocks.html: A row of short straight segments can cut through the true curve and change where it meets an axis or another line.

blocks.title: Read both inputs at a quadratic height
blocks.prompt: Use the graph of \(y=x^{2}+2x-2\) to estimate the x-values when \(y=1\). Give your answers to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Compare the plotted graph with the horizontal line \(y=1\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-3.0,\quad 1.0\).

blocks.html: Add extra table positions near a bend if the original spacing is too large to guide the curve.

sections.title: What do I report when one height meets the curve twice?
sections.label: Read both intersections
sections.intro: For a stated height, scan the whole plotted curve on a horizontal line at that height. A single height can give two inputs.

blocks.html: Read the x-coordinate of each crossing. For roots, the height is zero. An intercept is the coordinate pair on the axis, while the root itself is its x-value.

blocks.title: Read the two x-intercepts of a quadratic
blocks.prompt: Use the graph of \(y=x^{2}+2x-3\) to estimate the x-values when \(y=0\). Give your answers to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Use the horizontal axis, where \(y=0\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-3.0,\quad 1.0\).

blocks.html: Reading only the first crossing can omit a second valid solution on the other side.

blocks.title: Read two values at the same height on a quadratic
blocks.prompt: From the plot of \(y=-x^{2}+4\), choose the common height at \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\).
blocks.hint: Read both input positions on the horizontal axis.
blocks.solution:
Use the vertical guides at \(-1\) and \(1\).

Their heights on the curve agree. Both are \(3\).

blocks.html: Read an approximate value at a precision supported by the grid, and report both readings if both are required.

igcse-0580-graphs-functions-reciprocal-p.description: Evaluate a reciprocal table for nonzero inputs, draw its two branches and read coordinate pairs.

sections.title: Why does zero have no table value?
sections.label: Separate the allowable inputs
sections.intro: In \(y=\frac{a}{x}\), the input is the number underneath the fraction bar. The rule works for every nonzero input.

blocks.html: Leave the entry at \(x=0\) undefined. Compute the values for negative and positive inputs separately before plotting.

blocks.title: Complete a positive reciprocal table on both sides
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=\frac{8}{x}\) for \(x\ne0\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(y\)\(-2\)?\(-8\)?\(4\)\(2\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Divide the numerator by the signed input. Values at opposite nonzero inputs have opposite signs.

For \(x=-2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-4\).

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=8\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(y\)\(-2\)\(-4\)\(-8\)\(8\)\(4\)\(2\)

blocks.html: Writing zero as the output at this missing input would put a false point on the graph.

blocks.title: Complete a table for a negative reciprocal
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=\frac{-8}{x}\) for \(x\ne0\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(y\)?\(4\)\(8\)\(-8\)?\(-2\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
A negative numerator gives positive outputs at negative inputs and negative outputs at positive inputs.

For \(x=-4\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=2\).

For \(x=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-4\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(y\)\(2\)\(4\)\(8\)\(-8\)\(-4\)\(-2\)

blocks.html: Write ‘undefined’ for a zero denominator in a table, unless the question shows a blank excluded position.

sections.title: How do I draw both sides of the graph?
sections.label: Plot each continuous branch
sections.intro: Draw the negative-input branch using its table values, then draw the positive-input branch. Each branch is continuous over its own set of inputs.

blocks.html: Leave a gap between the branches at the vertical axis. With a negative numerator, positive and negative inputs still give opposite signs, but the two branches switch their vertical positions.

figure.alt: Two plotted branches are separated by the vertical axis. The left branch is above the horizontal axis and the right branch is below.
figure.caption: The rule has a negative numerator. At x equal to −2 the output is 4, while at x equal to 2 it is −4.

blocks.title: Handle the excluded input in a reciprocal table
blocks.prompt: The rule is \(y=\frac{4}{x}\) for \(x\ne0\). What belongs in the table at \(x=0\)?
blocks.hint: Ask whether zero is allowed in a denominator.
blocks.solution:
Substituting zero gives a denominator of \(0\).

Division by zero is undefined. Leave that cell unavailable and the two branches separate.

blocks.html: A line through the origin would add a value where the reciprocal is undefined.

sections.title: Where do I look for roots on a graph?
sections.label: Read where the output is zero
sections.intro: An equation of the form \(f(x)=0\) asks when the graph of the rule is on the horizontal axis. It can cross or touch that axis.

blocks.html: Mark the positions where the curve meets the x-axis. Project these points onto its numbered scale. Give the x-values, keeping every solution in the stated interval.

blocks.title: Estimate two roots from the x-axis
blocks.prompt: Use the graph of \(y=x^{2}+2x-4\) to estimate the x-values when \(y=0\). Give your answers to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Use the horizontal axis, where \(y=0\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-3.2,\quad 1.2\).

blocks.html: The curve meeting the vertical axis tells you its output at zero. That is only a root if the output there is also zero.

blocks.title: Estimate every solution at a fixed height
blocks.prompt: Use the graph of \(y=-x^{2}+3\) to estimate the x-values when \(y=-3\). Give your answers to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Compare the plotted graph with the horizontal line \(y=-3\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-2.4,\quad 2.4\).

blocks.html: Use an approximation sign when the graph reading is estimated.

sections.title: Which line gives a specified output?
sections.label: Compare the curve with a horizontal line
sections.intro: An equation of the form \(f(x)=k\) asks when the curve has height \(k\). Draw the horizontal line at that height.

blocks.html: Read each intersection with the curve. For example, to use \(y=x^2-x+1\) to solve \(x^2-x-2=0\), add 3 to make the comparison \(y=3\).

figure.alt: The teal quadratic and the orange horizontal line at height three cross twice on a scaled grid.
figure.caption: The horizontal line at height 3 compares both branches of the quadratic. The two solutions are the horizontal readings.

blocks.title: Match a changed equation to the right horizontal line
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=x^{2}+2\) and a horizontal comparison line. Use them to solve \(x^{2}-6=0\) to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
The requested equation is equivalent to \(x^{2}+2=8\). Read where the curve meets \(y=8\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-2.4,\quad 2.4\).

blocks.html: A pencilled guide from an intersection goes vertically to the x-axis. A horizontal guide goes to the y-axis and gives the output.

blocks.title: Use an auxiliary sloping line to solve an equation
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=x^{2}+5x-5\) with a second straight line. Use the graph to estimate both solutions of \(x^{2}-2=0\) to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
The equation is equivalent to setting \(x^{2}+5x-5\) equal to \(5x-3\). The extra line is \(y=5x-3\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-1.4,\quad 1.4\).

blocks.html: Find every intersection before giving an answer. Check the given interval and the scale.

sections.title: When do I need a sloping comparison line?
sections.label: Rearrange to match the plotted rule
sections.intro: If a related equation contains x-terms outside the supplied function, rearrange so one side is exactly the plotted expression.

blocks.html: Plot the expression on the other side as a second line. For solutions in x, read the x-values of the intersections. When asked for intersection points, give their full ordered pairs.

blocks.title: Read the root in the plotted interval
blocks.prompt: Only the part of \(y=x^{2}-3\) with \(0\leq x\leq 4\) is shown. Estimate the solution of \(x^{2}-3=0\) on that interval to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Use the horizontal axis, where \(y=0\).

Project the intersection onto the x-axis. The reading is approximately \(1.7\).

blocks.html: A line with the correct intercept but wrong slope can look close and give different roots. Use two points to draw it accurately.

blocks.title: Read each intersection as a complete ordered pair
blocks.prompt: Read both intersection points of \(y=x^{2}+3x-1\) and \(y=x+2\) from the graph.
blocks.hint: Keep the x- and y-coordinates from the same crossing together.
blocks.solution:
Find both places where the line crosses the curve.

Read each crossing as a pair, giving the first and second points \(\left(-3,-1\right)\) and \(\left(1,3\right)\).

blocks.html: Take the level or line from the algebra, then use the graph to estimate the numbers.

solution: Use the horizontal axis, where \(y=0\).

igcse-0580-graphs-functions-cubic-plots.description: Build tables for cubic rules and combinations of powers, plot them smoothly and find their numerical solutions.

sections.title: How do the terms contribute to a cubic table?
sections.label: Combine the powers at one input
sections.intro: A cubic table can include a cube, a squared or linear term, and a constant. Work through all the terms at the same input before moving to the next column.

blocks.html: At \(x=-2\), \(x^3=-8\) and \(x^2=4\). An outside negative coefficient changes the sign after evaluating the power.

blocks.title: Complete a table for a cubic and a constant
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=\frac{1}{2}x^{3}\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(-4\)?\(0\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)?
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Cubing a negative input gives a negative result. Apply the outside coefficient after cubing.

For \(x=-1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-\frac{1}{2}\).

For \(x=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=4\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(-4\)\(-\frac{1}{2}\)\(0\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(4\)

blocks.html: A positive number from the square does not make the whole output positive. Combine the signed contributions.

blocks.title: Use a table for a three-term cubic
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=x^{3}-2x\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)?\(1\)\(0\)?\(4\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Evaluate each term separately, then add them with their signs.

For \(x=-2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-4\).

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-1\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(-4\)\(1\)\(0\)\(-1\)\(4\)

blocks.html: At \(x=0\), every positive-power term vanishes. The constant is the output. Keep fractional coefficients exact while completing the table.

sections.title: Where can I add useful table points?
sections.label: Connect the plotted points smoothly
sections.intro: Plot a point for each column. Check whether the curve changes direction between adjacent positions and calculate more values near a bend if needed.

blocks.html: A smooth curve should pass through the calculated points on the stated interval. The rest of the curve can lie outside the printed window.

figure.alt: A cubic is plotted with five table points. As x increases, the curve rises, falls and rises again.
figure.caption: The table crosses guide the middle of the curve. Extra values near the changes of direction can improve a plot.

blocks.title: Read cubic mixtures with a squared term
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=-x^{3}+2x^{2}-1\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)?\(2\)\(-1\)\(0\)?
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
At a negative input, the square is positive but the cube is negative before its outside sign.

For \(x=-2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=15\).

For \(x=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-1\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(15\)\(2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(-1\)

blocks.html: Several points may have the same y-value. They belong at different x-positions.

blocks.title: Read a numerical height on a cubic
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=-x^{3}+2x+2\). Read the value of \(y\) at \(x=-1\).
blocks.hint: Start at the given input on the horizontal axis. Read the other coordinate at the graph.
blocks.solution:
Find \(x=-1\) on the horizontal scale.

Move vertically to the graph and then horizontally to the vertical scale. The point is \(\left(-1,1\right)\).

blocks.html: Use the full displayed interval when reading roots, including the central part of the curve.

sections.title: How do I find every intersection with a line?
sections.label: Read all displayed solutions
sections.intro: Use the steps from graphical equations. Rewrite the requested equation as the given rule equal to a line.

blocks.html: Plot the line to scale. Read the x-value of each intersection. A cubic can give several distinct readings on the same horizontal level or sloping line.

blocks.title: Find all displayed roots of a cubic
blocks.prompt: Use the graph of \(y=x^{3}-3x\) to estimate the x-values when \(y=0\). Give your answers to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Use the horizontal axis, where \(y=0\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-1.7,\quad 0.0,\quad 1.7\).

blocks.html: Stopping after the first crossing loses other solutions. A root at zero should be included when it satisfies the equation.

blocks.title: Use a line and a cubic to find three solutions
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=x^{3}+x\) and an additional line. Use the graph to estimate all solutions of \(x^{3}-3x=0\) to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Add \(4x\) to both sides of the requested equation. Use the intersection of \(y=x^{3}+x\) and \(y=4x\).

Project each intersection onto the x-axis. The readings in order are approximately \(-1.7,\quad 0.0,\quad 1.7\).

blocks.html: Keep all distinct readings in order of x and check the stated interval.

\(y\)\(3\)?\(-1\)\(-\frac{3}{2}\)?
solution: Cubing a negative input gives a negative result. Apply the outside coefficient after cubing.
For \(x=-1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-\frac{1}{2}\).
For \(x=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-5\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(3\)\(-\frac{1}{2}\)\(-1\)\(-\frac{3}{2}\)\(-5\)

\(y\)?\(-1\)\(-1\)?\(5\)

For \(x=-2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-7\).
For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-1\).

sections.title: Which inputs do the two root rules allow?
sections.label: Keep the real root defined
sections.intro: A positive half power means the real nonnegative square root. Its input must be at least zero.

blocks.html: Write \(x^{\frac12}=\sqrt{x}\quad\text{and}\quad x^{-\frac12}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\). The reciprocal needs strictly positive inputs because its denominator cannot be zero.

figure.alt: A square-root curve begins at the origin and passes through three marked points at x one, four and nine.
figure.caption: Use inputs such as 0, 1, 4, 9 and 16 to obtain simple exact outputs for the square-root table.

blocks.title: Plot a positive square-root rule
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=2\sqrt{x}\) for \(x\geq0\).

\(x\)\(0\)\(1\)\(4\)\(9\)\(16\)
\(y\)\(0\)?\(4\)?\(8\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
The half power is the nonnegative square root. This rule includes x equal to zero.

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=2\).

For \(x=9\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=6\).

\(x\)\(0\)\(1\)\(4\)\(9\)\(16\)
\(y\)\(0\)\(2\)\(4\)\(6\)\(8\)

blocks.html: A missing negative-input branch for a square-root rule is not a drawing omission. The real rule cannot give those outputs.

blocks.title: Complete a reciprocal-square-root table
blocks.prompt:

\(x\)\(1\)\(4\)\(9\)\(16\)\(25\)
\(y\)?\(3\)?\(\frac{3}{2}\)\(\frac{6}{5}\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Take the nonnegative root first. Since it is in a denominator, x must be strictly positive.

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=6\).

For \(x=9\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=2\).

\(x\)\(1\)\(4\)\(9\)\(16\)\(25\)
\(y\)\(6\)\(3\)\(2\)\(\frac{3}{2}\)\(\frac{6}{5}\)

blocks.html: Include zero in a square-root table only when it is allowed by the actual formula.

sections.title: How do I plot an inverse square?
sections.label: Use separate branches and the actual signs
sections.intro: A power of minus two gives the reciprocal of the square. Compute the squared input before division.

blocks.html: For \(y=ax^{-2}=\frac{a}{x^2}\), both signs of a nonzero input are allowed and have the same square. The two branches do not join at zero.

blocks.title: Read both sides of a reciprocal-square function
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=\frac{8}{x^{2}}\) for \(x\ne0\).

\(y\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)?\(8\)?\(2\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
The denominator is the square of x, so opposite inputs have the same denominator and output.

For \(x=-2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=2\).

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=8\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(y\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(2\)\(8\)\(8\)\(2\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)

blocks.html: A reciprocal square is distinct from the ordinary reciprocal. Opposite inputs have equal outputs, not opposite outputs, in this rule.

blocks.title: Evaluate a sum of two negative powers
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=\frac{3}{x}+\frac{8}{x^2}\) for \(x\ne0\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(y\)?\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(5\)\(11\)?\(\frac{5}{4}\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Evaluate each fraction separately. The first denominator keeps the sign of x, and the squared denominator does not.

For \(x=-4\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=-\frac{1}{4}\).

For \(x=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=\frac{7}{2}\).

\(x\)\(-4\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(y\)\(-\frac{1}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(5\)\(11\)\(\frac{7}{2}\)\(\frac{5}{4}\)

blocks.html: Check a pair of opposite inputs before plotting each side of zero.

sections.title: What if two different powers appear together?
sections.label: Use common allowable inputs
sections.intro: Read each term to see which inputs are allowed. Use only inputs that make all terms defined, then calculate the terms independently.

blocks.html: In \(y=\frac2x+\frac4{x^2}\), use nonzero inputs, including both signs. The two terms can have different signs for a negative input.

blocks.title: Identify inputs that a root-based graph allows
blocks.prompt: Which stated set of inputs gives real outputs for \(y=2\sqrt{x}\)?
blocks.hint: First check the square root, then check whether it is in a denominator.

A real square root requires \(x\geq0\).

blocks.html: Do not combine the two denominators mentally before checking whether the original rule allows the input.

igcse-0580-graphs-functions-exponential-.description: Build exponential tables and use a scaled graph to read initial values and growth or decay thresholds.

sections.title: How do I build a shifted exponential table?
sections.label: Evaluate the power first
sections.intro: In \(y=ab^x+c\), the variable is in the exponent. Compute the power, then multiply by a and add c.

blocks.html: At \(x=0\), \(b^0=1\) and the output is \(a+c\). Negative inputs may give fractional values. Retain these until plotting.

blocks.title: Complete a shifted exponential table
blocks.prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=3^{x}+3\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(\frac{28}{9}\)?\(4\)?\(12\)
blocks.hint: Substitute the x-value into every term of the expression. Retain the sign when using a negative input.
blocks.solution:
Evaluate the base to the given power first, multiply by the coefficient, then add the shift. A negative power gives a reciprocal.

For \(x=-1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=\frac{10}{3}\).

For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=6\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(\frac{28}{9}\)\(\frac{10}{3}\)\(4\)\(6\)\(12\)

blocks.html: A constant outside the exponent does not change the base or the exponent.

blocks.title: Plot a repeated-growth model

\(t\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(N\)\(3\)?\(27\)?
blocks.hint: Evaluate the power using the given time before multiplying by the starting amount.
blocks.solution:
At t equal to zero, the factor is one. Every whole hour multiplies the number by \(3\).

For \(t=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(N=9\).

For \(t=3\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(N=81\).

\(t\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(N\)\(3\)\(9\)\(27\)\(81\)

blocks.html: Use the table to choose a useful vertical scale before plotting.

sections.title: How does a repeated multiplier appear on a graph?
sections.label: Plot growth and decay of a model
sections.intro: In a simple growth model, the amount is multiplied by the same factor greater than one each time unit. In decay the multiplier lies between zero and one.

blocks.html: The amount at time zero sets the first point. To model halving each hour, use a factor of \(\frac12\) per hour, or a power \(2^{-t}\).

\(M\)?\(8\)?\(2\)
blocks.hint: Evaluate the power using the given time before multiplying by the starting amount.
blocks.solution:
Each whole hour halves the current mass. The curve falls as time increases.

For \(t=0\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(M=16\).

For \(t=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(M=4\).

\(t\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(M\)\(16\)\(8\)\(4\)\(2\)

blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.

Project the intersection onto the t-axis. The reading is approximately \(1.6\) hours.

blocks.html: Label time and the measured quantity. Use only the time domain described in the setting.

sections.intro: Find the threshold on the vertical scale and draw the horizontal guide. The crossing identifies when the model first attains the threshold.

blocks.html: Trace down to the time axis. Give a number with its time unit and a precision supported by the axis divisions.

figure.alt: The amount begins at 12 and follows a decreasing curve. An orange horizontal line marks the threshold at 3.
figure.caption: The vertical scale is mass in grams and the horizontal scale is time in hours. The threshold at 3 g is reached at 2 hours.

blocks.title: Read a threshold from a decay curve
blocks.prompt: The graph models the mass \(M=20\times 2^{-t}\) in grams remaining after t hours. Estimate the time at which the mass falls to 8 g, to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Move from the height \(M=8\) to the curve before reading time.

Project the intersection onto the t-axis. The reading is approximately \(1.3\) hours.

blocks.html: The threshold itself is an amount, not a time. Its numerical value does not belong on the horizontal axis.

blocks.title: Estimate an input to a shifted exponential
blocks.prompt: The graph shows \(y=2\times 3^{x}-2\). Estimate the solution of \(2\times 3^{x}-2=1\) to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Read the horizontal coordinate of each intersection. Check the full plotted interval.
blocks.solution:
Compare the plotted curve with the horizontal line at \(y=1\).

Project the intersection onto the x-axis. The reading is approximately \(0.4\).

blocks.html: For a question about whole time units, decide whether to use the first complete time after the threshold or the last one before it.

examples.title: Complete a shifted exponential table
examples.question:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(y=\frac{1}{2}\times 2^{x}+2\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(\frac{17}{8}\)?\(\frac{5}{2}\)?\(4\)
solution: Evaluate the base to the given power first, multiply by the coefficient, then add the shift. A negative power gives a reciprocal.
For \(x=-1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=\frac{9}{4}\).
For \(x=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(y=3\).

\(x\)\(-2\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(y\)\(\frac{17}{8}\)\(\frac{9}{4}\)\(\frac{5}{2}\)\(3\)\(4\)

examples.title: Plot a repeated-growth model
examples.question:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(N=2\times 2^{t}\) for a model of the number of sample colonies after t hours.

\(t\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(N\)\(2\)?\(8\)?
solution: At t equal to zero, the factor is one. Every whole hour multiplies the number by \(2\).
For \(t=1\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(N=4\).
For \(t=3\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(N=16\).

\(t\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(N\)\(2\)\(4\)\(8\)\(16\)

examples.title: Plot an exponential decay model
examples.question:
Complete the missing entries in the table for \(M=8\times 2^{-t}\) for the mass in grams remaining t hours after a process begins.

\(t\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(M\)?\(4\)?\(1\)
solution: Each whole hour halves the current mass. The curve falls as time increases.
For \(t=0\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(M=8\).
For \(t=2\), substitute that input into the rule. It gives \(M=2\).

\(t\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(M\)\(8\)\(4\)\(2\)\(1\)

examples.title: Use an exponential growth curve to read a time
examples.question: The graph models \(N=4\times 2^{t}\) sample colonies after t hours. Estimate when the count reaches 10 colonies. Give the time to one decimal place.
solution: Start at the threshold \(N=10\) and draw the horizontal comparison line.
Project the intersection onto the t-axis. The reading is approximately \(1.3\) hours.

glossary.definition: A rule in which the input is in an exponent.
The number multiplying the amount each time unit in a growth model.
A multiplier between zero and one.
An amount used to read when a condition is first met.
The model output at time zero.

revision.body:
Evaluate the power first

Evaluate the power before multiplying or adding. At time zero the power equals one.

Plot growth and decay of a model

Repeated growth or decay uses a constant multiplier per time unit.

Read time from a horizontal level

Draw a horizontal line through the threshold and read the time of its intersection.

Example

The model \(M=12\times2^{-t}\) falls from 12 g at time zero to 3 g at 2 hours.

Check yourself

  • Find the initial value of \(N=8\times2^t\).
  • Which variable should you read for the time?

Answers 8, and the horizontal time coordinate.
revision.checks:
• A constant outside the exponent does not change the base or the exponent.
  • Halving subtracts different amounts from different starting values. A curve is needed to show the decay model.
  • The threshold itself is an amount, not a time. Its numerical value does not belong on the horizontal axis.
revision.examTip: For a question about whole time units, decide whether to use the first complete time after the threshold or the last one before it.
